title: Linear Regression
interviewAnswer: Linear regression models the target as a weighted sum of features and typically minimizes squared error. Know its assumptions, how coefficients are interpreted, and why multicollinearity/outliers can matter.
why: Linear regression is simple enough to derive but rich enough to test assumptions, loss functions, interpretation, regularization and statistical reasoning.
intuition: The model fits a plane through feature space. Each coefficient changes the predicted target by a constant amount per unit feature change, holding other features fixed.
deepDive: Ordinary least squares minimizes squared residuals. Under standard assumptions it has useful unbiasedness/inference properties, but prediction can still work when inference assumptions are imperfect. Multicollinearity makes coefficients unstable; nonlinear relationships require transformed features or other models; heteroscedasticity affects standard errors. Ridge/Lasso trade bias for stability/sparsity.
math:
ŷ = Xβ + b
OLS: minimize ||y-Xβ||₂²
Closed form when invertible: β̂=(XᵀX)^{-1}Xᵀy
workedExample: If house price increases roughly linearly with area but location shifts the baseline, include both area and encoded location. A strong coefficient does not by itself prove area causally changes price.
code:
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
m=LinearRegression().fit(X_train,y_train)
print(m.coef_, m.intercept_)
commonMistakes: Saying linear regression requires every feature to be Normally distributed.
Interpreting coefficients causally without design assumptions.
followUps: What is R² and when can it mislead?
production: Monitor residual distribution, drift, coefficient stability and extrapolation. Linear models can be excellent baselines because they are cheap, interpretable and easy to debug.

lab.goal: Implement ordinary least squares with gradient descent, then compare it with scikit-learn.
lab.buildIt:
import numpy as np
rng=np.random.default_rng(0)
X=rng.normal(size=(200,1)); y=3*X[:,0]+2+rng.normal(0,.3,200)
Xb=np.c_[np.ones(len(X)),X]
w=np.zeros(2); lr=.05
for _ in range(1000):
    pred=Xb@w
    grad=(2/len(Xb))*Xb.T@(pred-y)
    w-=lr*grad
print('from scratch:',w)
lab.useIt:
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
m=LinearRegression().fit(X,y)
print('sklearn:',m.intercept_,m.coef_)
